title: The Effects of Lighting Design on Mood, Attention, and Stress

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Total Mood Disturbance (TMD) change score (post-session - pre-session) on POMS-SF
findings.mechanism: SAD and blue light conditions were expected to positively affect mood, creating a negative Total Mood Disturbance Score, while control was hypothesized to have no effect.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Total Mood Disturbance was not significantly different across light condition, F(2, 10) = 0.55, p = .58.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Depression-Dejection POMS subscale change score (post-session - pre-session)
findings.mechanism: Control condition was numerically slightly less effective at reducing depressive mood than SAD or blue light conditions, as expected if SAD and blue light were effective.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Depression-Dejection was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) =0.089, p =.92.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Fatigue POMS subscale change score (post-session - pre-session)
findings.mechanism: Blue light condition was numerically the least effective at reducing fatigue, contrary to the expectation that it would reduce melatonin production and fatigue.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that Fatigue was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.14, p= .34.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Change in heart rate from pre-session to mid-session
findings.mechanism: SAD condition was hypothesized to show a larger change in heart rate, indicating more physiological stress.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that change in heart rate from pre-session to mid-session was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,9) = 1.49, p= .25.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Change in heart rate from pre-session to post-session
findings.mechanism: Numeric pattern implies a link between a slightly elevated heart rate and the control condition compared to SAD and blue light conditions.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that change in heat rate pre-session to post-session was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) =0.044, p= .96.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Average reaction time in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: SAD condition was hypothesized to result in slower reaction times than blue light and control conditions due to potential distraction and irritation.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that average reaction time during the CCPT was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.34, p = .28.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Standard deviation of reaction times in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: Numerically, response times varied less in the blue light condition, potentially indicating more consistent attention, but results were inconclusive.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that the standard deviation of reaction times during the CCPT was not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 1.18, p= .33.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Percentage of omission errors in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: SAD condition was hypothesized to result in increased error rates due to potential distraction and irritation.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that omission errors were not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 0.5, p=.62.

findings.antecedent: light condition (bright, white SAD light; dim, warm control light; dim, 450nm blue light)
findings.consequent: Percentage of commission errors in Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT)
findings.mechanism: Color discrimination might have been more difficult in the blue light condition due to after-images, potentially explaining the numeric pattern.
findings.quote: A one-way ANOVA indicated that commission errors were not significantly different across light condition, F(2,10) = 0.9, p=.42.

stimuli.description: A light therapy condition with a 10,000 lux, 6500°K white light; a blue light condition with a 50 lux 450 nm light; and a control condition with a 50 lux 3500°K standard office light.

Visual stimuli for the Conjunctive Continuous Performance Task (CCPT) including four distinct shapes (square, circle, triangle, star) and four distinct colors (red, blue, green, yellow). Target was a red square.

limitations: Small sample size (N=11) leading to insufficient statistical power to detect genuine differences.
Experimental procedures might not have been sensitive enough or were flawed.
Extraneous variables such as weather patterns (non-uniform cloudy/sunny days) influenced participants' mood or stress levels.
Variations in time of day for sessions, with stronger effects potentially missed due to few evening sessions.
Variations in time of semester (normal week, midterms, spring break) affected participant workload, stress, and sleep patterns.

Measures might have been unfit: CCPT might not target the specific type of attention affected by lighting; POMS-SF might not be sensitive enough or included irrelevant subscales, and participants found adjectives synonymous or unfamiliar.
Participants might have remembered and intentionally maintained consistency in POMS-SF responses across repeated administrations within a session.
Heart rate might not fully capture physiological arousal as precisely as skin conductance or cortisol, and was easily influenced by researcher presence.
Possibility of a genuine null effect, suggesting previous literature might have erroneously reported or exaggerated lighting effects due to methodological issues.
Subjective opinions and personal preferences for lighting conditions might have influenced participant psychological states.
